Oxygen Saturation

Oxygen saturation, also known as SpO2, is a vital sign that measures the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is saturated with oxygen. It is an important indicator of a patient's oxygenation status and is commonly used to assess patients with respiratory or cardiovascular conditions.

Definition

Oxygen saturation is defined as the ratio of oxyhemoglobin to total hemoglobin in the blood. It is usually measured using a pulse oximeter, a non-invasive device that uses light to detect changes in blood oxygen levels.

Types/Classification

There are two main types of oxygen saturation: arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) and venous oxygen saturation (SvO2). Arterial oxygen saturation measures the oxygen saturation of arterial blood, while venous oxygen saturation measures the oxygen saturation of venous blood.

Mechanism/Pathophysiology

The mechanism of oxygen saturation involves the binding of oxygen to hemoglobin in the blood. Hemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the to the body's tissues. When oxygen binds to hemoglobin, it forms oxyhemoglobin, which is the oxygen-rich form of hemoglobin.

The normal range for oxygen saturation is 95-100%. A value below 90% is considered hypoxemia, which can lead to tissue hypoxia and other complications.

Clinical Features

The clinical features of low oxygen saturation include:

  • Shortness of breath
  • Chest pain
  • Confusion
  • Dizziness
  • Headache

Management

The management of low oxygen saturation depends on the underlying cause. Treatment options include:

  • Oxygen therapy: 2-4 L/min via nasal cannula or 5-10 L/min via face mask
  • Positioning: elevating the head of the bed to 30-40 degrees
  • Medications: bronchodilators such as albuterol or ipratropium

Nursing Care

Nursing care for patients with low oxygen saturation includes:

  • Monitoring: continuous monitoring of vital signs and oxygen saturation
  • Oxygen therapy: administering oxygen as prescribed and monitoring for response
  • Positioning: positioning the patient to optimize breathing and oxygenation
  • Education: educating the patient and family on oxygen therapy and breathing techniques

A helpful mnemonic to remember the steps for managing low oxygen saturation is POSITION:

  • P: Position the patient to optimize breathing
  • O: Oxygen therapy as prescribed
  • S: Support the patient with medications and interventions
  • I: Inform and educate the patient and family
  • T: Titrate oxygen therapy as needed
  • I: Implement breathing techniques and relaxation methods
  • O: Observe and monitor for response and complications
  • N: Notify the healthcare team of any changes or concerns

Key Points for NORCET Exam

Key points to remember for the NORCET exam include:

  • Normal range for oxygen saturation: 95-100%
  • Hypoxemia: oxygen saturation below 90%
  • Oxygen therapy: 2-4 L/min via nasal cannula or 5-10 L/min via face mask
  • Positioning: elevating the head of the bed to 30-40 degrees
  • Medications: bronchodilators such as albuterol or ipratropium
